Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
0. Scope, conventions, and main conclusions
This note derives the four vertex contributions to the many-body Berry phase in two
independent ways. The first uses leg-specific antiunitary symmetries and real gauges.
The second uses the Bloch/Nambu representation of the unitary symmetry at each vertex
and evaluates its ground-state eigenvalue momentum sector by momentum sector. The
final sections extend the real-gauge argument to Gutzwiller-projected states.
The Wilson-loop convention and the real pairing interpolation matter. I use normalized
ground-state overlaps and a real seam-pairing function s(φ), either the piecewise-linear
interpolation or cos(φ). The earlier complex pairing phase exp(iφ) does not possess the
same leg-specific antiunitary symmetries, so the vertex derivation below does not apply
unchanged to that path.
The individual vertex phases are gauge/sign dependent. The ground-state eigenvalues
u_v, the relation T_v²=u_v, and the total Wilson loop modulo 2π are the robust
statements. In particular, u_3=+1 permits both T_3=+1 and T_3=−1; continuous
real-gauge tracking selects the latter in the convention used here.
1. Model, twist path, and Wilson loop
1.1 Bloch/Nambu Hamiltonian
The normal block is the two-orbital Chern-insulator Hamiltonian. The pairing block
contains intraorbital p-wave terms and interorbital s-wave pairing. Only the normal block
is needed in closed form for the final self-inverse momentum evaluation, but the full
structure determines the antiunitary symmetries on each leg.
The numerical implementation uses the corresponding real-space BdG Hamiltonian.
Hopping across the seam from site 0 to site 1 acquires exp(iφ_μ). The seam-pairing terms
are multiplied by the real function s(φ_μ). For the linear path, s decreases continuously
from +1 to −1 on 0≤φ≤π and returns from −1 to +1 on π≤φ≤2π. For the cosine path,
s(φ)=cosφ.
3

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
1.2 Closed trajectory and its four real structures
Figure 1. The four-leg twist loop. Each leg has its own reflection-conjugation symmetry. The last leg
requires a translated y-reflection.
At every interior point of a leg the ground state is nondegenerate and gapped. The
Hamiltonian closes at (2π,2π)=(0,0). The four vertices are denoted v_1=(π,0), v_2=(π,π),
v_3=(2π,π), and v_4=(2π,2π).
1.3 Gauge invariance of the discretized Wilson loop
Under an arbitrary rephasing of each state, a normalized link changes by endpoint
phases. On a closed loop these phases telescope, so the total product is invariant modulo
2π. This statement assumes that no link overlap vanishes; otherwise its phase is
undefined and the mesh or gauge must be repaired.
4

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
2. Symmetry-based Z₄ quantization
Before using the real gauges, it is useful to recall the more general path-symmetry
argument. Suppose a closed trajectory decomposes into Q trajectories C_j, and a
symmetry maps each C_j to C_{j+1} without reversing orientation. Then all loop phases
equal a common γ modulo 2π. If the concatenated trajectories cancel, their phases sum to
[1,2]
zero. These are the standard relations behind symmetry-adapted Z_Q Berry phases.
This argument constrains entire Wilson loops, not the local Berry connection at every
point. A particular leg may have nonzero smooth contributions in a particular gauge.
Exact quantization is a property of the symmetry-adapted closed path, not a generic
property of every interpolation between the same endpoints. For an actual Hamiltonian
family, the quantized sector can change only through a gap closing, loss of symmetry, or
a singular state family.
3. Approach I: leg-specific antiunitary symmetries
and real gauges
3.1 Explicit reflection-conjugation operators
Let K denote complex conjugation in the real-space fermion basis. Coordinates are
understood modulo L_x,L_y, and Q=diag(i,−i) acts on the orbital pair (c,d). The three
unitary spatial operations are:
Each operator squares to one. On the four legs, the antiunitary symmetry is respectively
Θ_x, Θ_y, Θ_x, and Θ_y^(x). Complex conjugation reverses a hopping phase, while the
reflection exchanges the two bond orientations and restores the original term. The orbital
matrix Q supplies the signs needed by the interorbital hopping terms. Reality of s(φ) is
essential.
5

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
3.2 Antiunitary eigenphase and construction of a real state
Because the ground state is unique on a leg, it is an eigenstate of that leg's antiunitary
operation. The eigenvalue is a phase A_l(λ). Multiplying the state by its square root
produces a state invariant under the same antiunitary operation.
3.3 Why the interior of every leg has zero Berry connection
Normalization forces the real part of the diagonal connection to vanish. Reality forces the
whole diagonal matrix element to be real. Therefore it vanishes identically. Nearby
overlaps within one leg are real and, after choosing continuous signs, positive.
The full loop phase is consequently located at the four points where the real structure
changes. This is a transition-function construction: the smooth phase inside each patch
vanishes, but patches must be glued nontrivially. Real-gauge obstructions of this general
[3]
type are also central to Stiefel–Whitney descriptions of real band structures.
3.4 Vertex transition functions and the unitary U_v
At a vertex, the same ground state has one real representation from the incoming leg and
another from the outgoing leg. Their normalized overlap is the vertex transition function
T_v.
Since both antiunitary operations are symmetries at the vertex, their product is a unitary
symmetry. Its ground-state eigenvalue is exactly the ratio of antiunitary amplitudes.
6

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
3.5 Explicit vertex unitaries and the role of fermion parity
Vertex Unitary product Spatial action Orbital
action
v₁=(π,0) R_yR_x (x,y)→(1−x,1−y) Q
v₂=(π,π) R_xR_y (x,y)→(1−x,1−y) Q
v₃=(2π,π) T_xR_yR_x (x,y)→(2−x,1−y) Q
v₄=(2π,2π) R_xT_xR_y (x,y)→(−x,1−y) Q
Every spatial map squares to the identity, while Q²=−I. Hence the single-particle unitary
squares to −I. Its many-body lift squares to fermion parity, because conjugating every
annihilation operator by −1 is precisely the adjoint action of fermion parity.
Thus every vertex transition function is a fourth root of unity. The sign u_v itself is not
fixed by the operator algebra alone: it is a quantum number of the ground state. Sections
3.6 and 4 evaluate that sign in two different representations.
3.6 Evaluating the antiunitary amplitude from a fixed Slater
reference
In the numerical real-gauge approach, the Gaussian state is represented about one
common Slater reference |F⟩. For modes in the reference occupation set, a particle-hole
transformation d=c† is used; otherwise d=c. The state is then written in BCS form:
The numerator is evaluated from the amplitude of the reflected reference configuration.
If a configuration S differs from F on an even mode set I=S△F, its amplitude is a
basis-ordering sign times a Pfaffian minor of Z. Reflection also supplies orbital phases
and a fermionic permutation sign.
7

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
This construction is not an additional physical approximation; it is a convenient way to
evaluate the antiunitary eigenphase of a Gaussian state. At the fourth vertex, for
example, A_out=−A_in, giving u_4=−1. At the first three vertices, the same evaluation
gives u_1=u_2=u_3=+1.
3.7 Continuous sign tracking and the third-vertex π
The relation T_v²=u_v fixes δ_v only modulo π. A real normalized state also has a sign
freedom. The branch is fixed by starting with a square root of A_l and then requiring
every interior real overlap to be positive. If an interior overlap is negative, the target real
state is multiplied by −1 and the process continues. At a vertex, the transition overlap is
not forced to be positive; its residual phase is the vertex contribution.
Vertex u_v Allowed T_v Continuous-gauge δ_v
T_v
v₁ +1 +1 or −1 +1 0
v₂ +1 +1 or −1 +1 0
v₃ +1 +1 or −1 −1 π
v₄ −1 +i or −i +i π/2
The third vertex is the important branch subtlety: u_3=+1 does not imply δ_3=0. The
continuously tracked real gauge selects T_3=−1, whose square is also +1. Flipping the
sign of a real state throughout an entire leg changes both adjacent vertex phases by π;
their product is unchanged, so the total Wilson loop remains invariant modulo 2π.
4. Approach II: Bloch-spinor and
momentum-sector derivation
4.1 Momentum representation of the vertex unitaries
All four spatial operations have the form S:r↦−r+r₀ and therefore map crystal momentum
k to −k. I define V_v(k) through its action on creation operators. The orbital factor
Q=diag(i,−i) and the reflection center r₀ determine a momentum-dependent phase.
For the fourth vertex, r₀=(0,1), so V_4(k)=exp(ik_y)Q. At a self-inverse momentum, k=−k
modulo a reciprocal lattice vector, exp(ik_y)=±1 and V_4(k)²=−I. Its two eigenvalues are
therefore ±i on single-particle states.
8

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
4.2 Which vertices contain self-inverse momenta?
Periodic boundary conditions allow k_μ=2πn_μ/L_μ. Antiperiodic boundary conditions
allow k_μ=2π(n_μ+1/2)/L_μ. A self-inverse momentum must satisfy 2k_μ=0 modulo 2π in
both directions. On the even lattices used here, antiperiodic directions contain no such
momentum.
Vertex x boundary y boundary Self-inverse sectors Result
v₁=(π,0) Antiperiodic Periodic None u₁=+1
v₂=(π,π) Antiperiodic Antiperiodic None u₂=+1
v₃=(2π,π) Periodic Antiperiodic None u₃=+1
v₄=(2π,2π) Periodic Periodic (0,0), (π,0), (0,π), (π,π) Evaluate
below
For a distinct ±k pair, the even BCS ground sector has U_v eigenvalue +1. One minus
sign comes from V_v(−k)V_v(k)=−I; another comes from exchanging the two fermionic
creation operators when k and −k are interchanged. Hence the first three vertices, which
have no self-inverse sectors, give u_1=u_2=u_3=+1. Only v₄ requires a nontrivial
ground-state representation analysis.
4.3 Normal and pairing Hamiltonian at a self-inverse momentum
At v₄, all self-inverse momenta have sin k_x=sin k_y=0. Therefore the spin-orbit terms
and p-wave pairing vanish. Only ξ(k)σ_z and the interorbital Δ_s pairing remain. In the
orbital basis (c_k,d_k), the normal energies are ξ and −ξ.
The local Fock space separates into odd and even parity sectors. This is a two-orbital
momentum-sector Hamiltonian, not a real-space exact-enumeration calculation. The odd
sector is governed directly by the two eigenvalues of h(k). The even sector consists of the
empty state and the doubly occupied c_k†d_k† pair state. Since tr h(k)=0, its two energies
are ±|Δ_s|.
Thus the momentum-sector ground state is odd when |ξ|>|Δ_s| and even when |ξ|<|Δ_s|.
Equality is a local gap closing. In an even sector, the empty and paired states both have
V_4 eigenvalue +1. In an odd sector, the lowest Bloch spinor is c for ξ<0 and d for ξ>0,
and its V_4 eigenvalue is respectively +i exp(ik_y) or −i exp(ik_y).
9

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
4.4 Explicit evaluation at m=−2
With t=1 and m=−2, the four values ξ=−2cos k_x−2cos k_y+2 are −2, +2, +2, and +6.
Their magnitudes all exceed Δ_s=1/2. Hence every self-inverse sector has an odd-parity
ground state. Four odd sectors together give the required even total fermion parity.
k ξ(k) Lowest odd spinor exp(ik_y) Sector
eigenvalue
(0,0) −2 c +1 +i
(π,0) +2 d +1 −i
(0,π) +2 d −1 +i
(π,π) +6 d −1 +i
Figure 2. Ground-state parity and U₄ eigenvalue in each self-inverse sector at the fourth vertex. The
product of the four sector eigenvalues is −1.
This reproduces the fixed-reference Gaussian/Pfaffian calculation and the direct
many-body symmetry expectation value. The derivation also explains why the result is
independent of the linear system size for the even periodic lattices considered: the same
four self-inverse momenta and the same local sector Hamiltonians occur for every such
size.
4.5 Why all four odd sectors do not imply an odd ground state
Each odd momentum sector has one occupied fermionic mode. Four such sectors
therefore contain four fermions and have even total parity. Their U₄ eigenvalues are ±i
rather than ±1, consistently with U₄²=(−1)^N: in an odd sector U₄²=−1, while in the full
even-parity ground state U₄²=+1. The product of the four ±i values is real and equals −1.
10

5. Combining the vertex data into the many-body
Berry phase
The real-gauge calculation and the Bloch-representation calculation provide the same
four squared transition functions. Choosing the continuously tracked branch described in
Section 3.7 gives:
A branch-independent partial check follows directly from the ground-state eigenvalues. It
determines the Berry phase modulo π; the oriented Wilson-loop convention and
continuous gauge determine the remaining sign modulo 2π.
5.1 Numerical reality and mesh checks
The real-gauge Wilson product was evaluated for linear, cosine, and interpolated real
pairing profiles and for M=4,8,16,32 mesh points per leg. After removing the legwise
antiunitary phases, the largest interior link phase was at the 10⁻¹⁵ scale. The vertex
phases remained (0,0,π,π/2), and their sum reproduced the original Berry phase to
floating-point precision.

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
6. Gutzwiller-projected states
6.1 Projected overlaps and Wilson loop
Let P_g be Hermitian and independent of the twist parameter λ. It may be a genuine
projector or a smooth interpolation such as exp(−gD). Define the unnormalized projected
state, its norm, and the normalized projected state as follows.
For a genuine projector P_g²=P_g, whereas for P_g=exp(−gD) the overlap contains
exp(−2gD). There is no generic reason for γ_g to equal the unprojected phase. Projection
changes configuration amplitudes and therefore changes both magnitudes and phases of
link overlaps. Projected-parton Berry phases constructed from such overlaps have
[4]
previously been evaluated by Monte Carlo sampling.
6.2 Sufficient condition for exact invariance under projection
The strong condition is that P_g respects every leg-specific antiunitary operation, not
merely that it is real or diagonal in one fixed occupation basis.
The projected norm is real, so the normalized projected state has exactly the same
antiunitary eigenphase A_l. Multiplying by A_l^(1/2) therefore makes it real on the same
leg. Interior Berry connections vanish just as in the unprojected case. It remains to show
that the vertex transition functions are also unchanged.
12

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
At a fixed vertex, the numerator is precisely the projected norm, so all projection
dependence cancels. This proves equality vertex by vertex, without relying only on
continuity in g. The proof requires nonzero projected norms, smooth states on each leg,
and nonzero link overlaps. It does not construct a projected parent Hamiltonian and
therefore does not by itself prove that the projected state is gapped.
6.3 Commutation with C₄ alone: a weaker statement
If instead C₄P_gC₄⁻¹=P_g, the relations among the four projected Wilson loops survive,
and trajectory cancellation is independent of projection. Hence Z₄ quantization survives.
At one isolated projected point, this symmetry alone does not explicitly identify the
sector. If a smooth nonsingular interpolation in g is also available, continuity together
with quantization prevents the sector from jumping along that family. The stronger
antiunitary commutation condition proves the same transition functions directly.
6.4 Why parton-type and double-occupancy projections can differ
The distinction is not simply correlated versus uncorrelated, or diagonal versus
off-diagonal. It is whether the complete symmetry structure of the path is preserved. The
parton-type projection used in our calculation preserved the Berry phase, consistently
with preservation of the leg-specific real structures. A double-occupancy penalty need not
do so.
The last expression equals exp(−gD) only if U_lD U_l†=D. When U_l changes the local
density or pairing structure, the condition can fail. A real diagonal factor leaves
configuration phases unchanged but can still destroy the leg-specific real gauge by
changing amplitudes. Interior overlaps then acquire imaginary parts and a smooth
nonquantized contribution is allowed. This is the general diagnostic consistent with our
two numerical behaviors; the commutators must be checked for each concrete
implementation.

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
6.5 Relation to Hetényi’s exact finite-g example
Hetényi studied a different geometric response, namely the current response of projected
variational wavefunctions. For a Gutzwiller-projected Fermi sea, the total-position shift
commutes with the double-occupancy operator, so the same geometric response is
obtained at finite projection strength. This is a special example of the same commutation
principle, not a universal theorem for all projections and twist paths.
[5]
Non-centrosymmetric or singular projectors can fall outside the argument.
7. Assumptions, failure modes, and physical
interpretation
7.1 Checklist for applying the vertex derivation
1. The ground state must be unique and gapped on every leg and at every vertex.
2. The seam-pairing function must be real for the stated reflection-conjugation
symmetries.
3. The correct orbital phases and the translation on the last leg must be included.
4. Fermion parity is essential when converting U_v²=−I into the allowed many-body
eigenvalues.
5. The square root of A_l and the signs of real states must be tracked continuously.
6. No normalized link overlap may vanish.
7. Only the total Berry phase modulo 2π is independent of the legwise sign conventions.
7.2 What the Berry phase does not prove
Equal Berry phases do not imply equal correlation functions, Gaussian character,
excitation spectra, adiabatic connectedness, or identical topological order. A projected
wavefunction can be strongly non-Gaussian while retaining exactly the same Wilson loop.
Likewise, the symmetry argument for a wavefunction family does not by itself establish a
gapped parent Hamiltonian or identify the full vortex response of a physical spin model.
The projected-parton literature also emphasizes the role of the background internal
[4]
gauge flux in obtaining the correct physical response.
7.3 Relation to a single fixed antiunitary symmetry
If one fixed antiunitary symmetry applied along the entire loop, a single real gauge could
[6]
be used everywhere and the total phase would be restricted to 0 or π. Our loop instead
uses different real structures on different legs. The transition functions between those
structures permit ±π/2 contributions and are the reason the Z₄ result is compatible with
legwise reality.
14

Many-body Berry phase: vertex representations and projection Technical summary
Appendix A. Detailed momentum-sector algebra
A.1 Deriving the phase exp(ik·r₀)
Use c_k=N_cell^(−1/2) Σ_r exp(−ik·r)c_r and S²=1 with S r=−r+r₀. Acting on a creation
operator and substituting r=S r′ gives exp(ik·r)=exp(ik·r₀)exp(−ik·r′). The remaining sum
is c_(−k)†. This proves V(k)=exp(ik·r₀)Q. The relation V(−k)V(k)=−I follows either from
Q²=−I or directly from U²=−I on single-particle states.
A.2 Even-sector energies at a self-inverse momentum
At self-inverse k, let |P⟩=c_k†d_k†|0⟩. The even subspace is spanned by |0⟩ and |P⟩. The
normal Hamiltonian contributes zero to |0⟩ and tr h(k) to |P⟩. The interorbital pairing
couples these two states with magnitude |Δ_s|. Thus the even Hamiltonian has trace tr h
and determinant −|Δ_s|², yielding the eigenvalues displayed in Section 4.3. The odd
subspace contains c_k†|0⟩ and d_k†|0⟩ and is governed directly by h(k). Comparing the
lowest energies of the two sectors determines the ground parity without constructing the
full real-space Fock space.
A.3 Sector symmetry eigenvalues
At v₄, V_4(k)=exp(ik_y)diag(i,−i). An even empty state has eigenvalue +1. The paired
state acquires the product of the c and d creation phases, namely exp(2ik_y)(i)(−i)=+1.
An odd c-occupied state has eigenvalue i exp(ik_y), while an odd d-occupied state has
eigenvalue −i exp(ik_y). These four rules are sufficient to reproduce every entry in the v₄
table.
